Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. For supplied finite-valued nonnegative measurable density representatives $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ in the convention of [[def-likelihood-density]], the **root-L2 Hellinger distance** is

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each

$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: By [A1], [F3], and [F4], take finite-valued nonnegative densities $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ for a common sigma-finite dominator $\mu$. Define $\rho(A):=P(A)+Q(A)$. For disjoint measurable $A_k$, countable additivity of $P,Q$ and regrouping nonnegative series give $\rho(\bigcup_kA_k)=\sum_k\rho(A_k)$; also $\rho(\varnothing)=0$ and $\rho(\mathsf X)=2$. Thus $\rho$ is a finite, hence sigma-finite, measure by [F6]. Additivity of the nonnegative integral [F10] gives $\rho(A)=\int_A(p+q)\,d\mu$, with $p+q$ measurable by [F7].

Using $p,q$ against $\mu$, the set $B:=\{p\ge q\}$ is measurable by [F7,F8]. On $B$, $p=(p-q)+q$, so additivity [F10] gives $\delta:=P(B)-Q(B)=\int_B(p-q)\,d\mu\ge0$. On $B^c$, $q=(q-p)+p$ and the total masses are one, hence $\int_{B^c}(q-p)\,d\mu=Q(B^c)-P(B^c)=\delta$. Additivity then gives $\int|p-q|\,d\mu=2\delta$. For any measurable $A$, the difference on $A\cap B$ lies in $[0,\delta]$ by monotonicity [F10], while the difference on $A\cap B^c$ lies in $[-\delta,0]$; thus $|P(A)-Q(A)|\le\delta$, and $A=B$ attains $\delta$. Therefore [F2] gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\delta=\tfrac12\int|p-q|\,d\mu$.

On $\{p+q>0\}$ define $\bar p=p/(p+q)$ and $\bar q=q/(p+q)$, and set both to zero on $\{p+q=0\}$. For $r<0$, $\{\bar p>r\}$ is the whole space; for $r\ge0$, it is $\{p+q>0\}\cap\{p-r(p+q)>0\}$. Thus [F7,F8] make $\bar p$ measurable, and the same argument applies to $\bar q$. Since $p=q=0$ where $p+q=0$, [F9] gives $\int_A\bar p\,d\rho=\int_A\bar p(p+q)\,d\mu=P(A)$ and $\int_A\bar q\,d\rho=Q(A)$ for every measurable $A$. Hence $\bar p,\bar q$ are finite-valued density representatives of $P,Q$ against $\rho$.

Pointwise $|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)$. Hölder [F5] therefore gives $\int|p-q|\,d\mu\le h(P,Q)\bigl(\int(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\bigr)^{1/2}$. The squared second factor is $2+2\int\sqrt{pq}\,d\mu\le4$, since [F5] applied to $\sqrt p,\sqrt q$ bounds their product integral by $1$. Step 1.2 now gives $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q)$.

Write $H_\lambda(P,Q)^2$ for the defining Hellinger integral computed from supplied densities against a common dominator $\lambda$. Applying [F1] and [F9] to the densities in step 2.1 gives $H_\rho(P,Q)^2=\int(\sqrt{\bar p}-\sqrt{\bar q})^2\,d\rho=\int_{\{p+q>0\}}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu=H_\mu(P,Q)^2$, because both original densities vanish where $p+q=0$. For any measure $\alpha$ and finite-valued nonnegative densities $f,g$ of the same finite measure $\Lambda$ with respect to $\alpha$, they agree $\alpha$-almost everywhere: on $E_m:=\{f\ge g+1/m\}$, equality of their density integrals gives $0=\int_{E_m}(f-g)\,d\alpha\ge\alpha(E_m)/m$, so $\alpha(E_m)=0$. Since $\{f>g\}=\bigcup_{m\ge1}E_m$, and the same argument with $f,g$ swapped handles $\{g>f\}$, this proves uniqueness almost everywhere. Thus changing supplied representatives against a fixed dominator does not change the Hellinger integral.

u, ar q_
u$ against the same finite measure $ho=P+Q$. The uniqueness argument in step 3.1 gives $ ar p_

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

For all $x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$,
$$\exp((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)\exp x+t\exp y.$$
If $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $x=y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.

Assume AC for the imported density-representative convention. Let $P,Q$ be probability laws on a measurable space, both dominated by one specified common sigma-finite positive measure. Then the root-L2 Hellinger distance from [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]] is independent of the choice of common dominating measure. With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q),\qquad h(P,Q)^2\le 2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: For $n\ge1$ put $L_n(\theta,x_{1:n})=\prod_{i=1}^np(\theta,x_i)$ and $Z_n(x_{1:n})=\int_\Theta L_n(\theta,x_{1:n})\,\Pi(d\theta)$. The coordinate maps into $\Theta\times\mathsf X$ are measurable by the product sigma-algebra definition [F20]; joint measurability of $p$ and closure under finite products [F23] make $L_n$ product-measurable. For each fixed $\theta$, repeated Tonelli [F6, F21] and $\int p(\theta,x)\,d\mu=1$ give $\int L_n(\theta,\cdot)\,d\mu^n=1$. By [F24], $L_n(\theta,\cdot)d\mu^n$ is a measure. On every measurable rectangle $\prod_{i=1}^n A_i$, repeated Tonelli and the density identity give mass $\prod_iP_\theta(A_i)$; this is also the rectangle mass of $P_\theta^n$ by [F8, F10]. Rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra [F20], and both are probability measures, so [F22], using the whole sample space as a finite-measure exhaustion, identifies these measures. Tonelli over $\Pi$ and $\mu^n$ now gives $\int Z_n\,d\mu^n=1$, hence $Z_n<\infty$ $\mu^n$-almost everywhere and $P_0^n$-almost surely.

Fix $0<a<b$, choose measurable $B_a\subseteq\{\theta:D(P_0\|P_\theta)<a\}$ with $\Pi(B_a)>0$, and let $\Pi_a$ be the normalized restriction of $\Pi$ to $B_a$. For each $\theta\in B_a$, finite KL gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$. Define $r_\theta=p_0/p(\theta,\cdot)$ where $p(\theta,\cdot)>0$ and zero elsewhere. Since $P_0(\{p(\theta,\cdot)=0\})=0$, direct integration of the two supplied densities gives $\int_A r_\theta\,dP_\theta=P_0(A)$ for every measurable $A$, so $r_\theta$ is a Radon–Nikodym derivative. Define $Z_\theta=\log(p(\theta,\cdot)/p_0)$ where both densities are positive and zero elsewhere; then $Z_\theta=-\log r_\theta$ $P_0$-almost surely. For $u\ge1$, [F19] gives $\log u\le u$, so $\mathbb E_0Z_\theta^+\le\int_{\{p(\theta,x)>p_0(x)\}}p(\theta,x)\,d\mu\le1$. Pinsker [F17] gives $D(P_0\|P_\theta)\ge0$, and [F5] yields $\mathbb E_0Z_\theta^-=D(P_0\|P_\theta)+\mathbb E_0Z_\theta^+\le a+1$. Thus $\mathbb E_0|Z_\theta|\le a+2$.

Fix $\eta>0$ with $V_\eta\ne\varnothing$, and let $\alpha_n=P_0^n\phi_n$ and $\beta_n=\sup_{\theta\in V_\eta}P_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)$. The two summable series imply $\alpha_n,\beta_n\to0$. Choose $m\ge1$ with $\alpha_m<1/4$ and $\beta_m<1/4$. For $\ell=\lfloor n/m\rfloor$, group the first $\ell m$ observations into disjoint consecutive blocks of length $m$. By [F8, F10] the block vectors are independent and identically distributed under each fixed IID law; [F9] makes $Y_j:=\phi_m(\text{block }j)$ independent $[0,1]$ random variables. Their means are at most $1/4$ under $P_0$ and at least $3/4$ under every $P_\theta$ with $\theta\in V_\eta$. Let $\widetilde\phi_n=\mathbf1\{\ell^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^\ell Y_j>1/2\}$ for $\ell\ge1$, and $0$ otherwise.

Since $P_0=P_{\theta_0}\ll\mu$, $p_0(X_i)>0$ for every sampled coordinate almost surely. On this event define the relative evidence $D_n=Z_n(X_{1:n})/\prod_{i=1}^np_0(X_i)$; it is finite $P_0^n$-almost surely by step 1.1.

Let $u(\theta,x)=p(\theta,x)/p_0(x)$ when both densities are positive and $0$ otherwise; the lift of $p_0$ to $\Theta\times\mathsf X$ is measurable by [F2,F20], and the piecewise quotient is measurable by [F23,F25]. Extend $Z(\theta,x)=\log u(\theta,x)$ on $u>0$ by $0$ on $u=0$. For every real $s$, its upper threshold is $\{u>\exp(s)\}$ if $s\ge0$ and $\{u=0\}\cup\{u>\exp(s)\}$ if $s<0$; [F27,F29] and [F25] therefore make $Z$ product-measurable. For each $\theta\in B_a$, [F5] identifies $D(P_0\|P_\theta)=-\mathbb E_0Z_\theta$; applying [F6] to the positive and negative parts shows that these section integrals, and hence $\theta\mapsto D(P_0\|P_\theta)$ on $B_a$, are measurable. Tonelli [F6] and the uniform bound in step 1.2 show $G(x):=\int Z(\theta,x)\,\Pi_a(d\theta)$ is finite for $P_0$-almost every $x$ and integrable, with $\mathbb E_0G=-\kappa$ where $\kappa:=\int D(P_0\|P_\theta)\,\Pi_a(d\theta)\le a$. For each $\theta\in B_a$, $P_0\{x:p(\theta,x)=0\}=0$; Tonelli [F6] applied to the measurable indicator of this set implies $\Pi_a\{\theta:p(\theta,X_i)=0\}=0$ almost surely for each coordinate $i$. Intersecting these probability-one events over all $i$, $\exp(\sum_{i=1}^nZ(\theta,X_i))=\prod_{i=1}^np(\theta,X_i)/p_0(X_i)$ for $\Pi_a$-almost every $\theta$ and every $n$. Set $G=0$ on the measurable $P_0$-null set where the integral is not finite.

For $\ell\ge1$, [F26] writes the exponential of the centered sum as a product; the finite product law [F10] and Tonelli [F6] factor its expectation, and [F12] bounds each factor by $e^{\lambda^2/8}$. Thus $\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda\sum_{j=1}^\ell(Y_j-\mathbb EY_j)\}\le e^{\ell\lambda^2/8}$. Under $P_0$, rejection requires an upward deviation greater than $\ell/4$; Markov [F15] with $\lambda=1$ gives $P_0^n\widetilde\phi_n\le e^{-\ell/8}$. Under every $P_\theta$ in $V_\eta$, nonrejection requires a downward deviation at least $\ell/4$; Markov with $\lambda=-1$ gives $P_\theta^n(1-\widetilde\phi_n)\le e^{-\ell/8}$. Since $\ell\ge n/m-1$, both errors are at most $e^{1/8}e^{-cn}$ for $c:=1/(8m)$ and all $n\ge m$.

The variables $G(X_i)$ are IID by [F8, F9] and integrable by step 2.2. The strong law [F11] gives $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nG(X_i)\to-\kappa$; because $\kappa\le a<b$, eventually $\sum_iG(X_i)>-nb$. Tonelli and the bound in step 1.2 also give $\int\sum_i|Z_\theta(X_i)|\,\Pi_a(d\theta)<\infty$ for $P_0^n$-almost every sample; the exponential is integrable by step 1.1. By step 2.2, the likelihood ratio in $D_n$ agrees with $\exp(\sum_iZ_\theta(X_i))$ for $\Pi_a$-almost every $\theta$, so $D_n\ge\Pi(B_a)\int\exp(\sum_iZ_\theta(X_i))\,\Pi_a(d\theta)$. Jensen [F13, F14] bounds this integral below by $\exp(\sum_iG(X_i))$, giving $D_n\ge\Pi(B_a)e^{-nb}$ eventually.

The product-density identity in step 1.1 and Tonelli [F6] imply $\mathbb E_{P_0^n}A_n=\int_{V_\eta}P_\theta^n((1-\widetilde\phi_n)\mathbf1_{\{p_0(X_i)>0\,\forall i\}})\,\Pi(d\theta)\le e^{1/8}e^{-cn}$ for $n\ge m$, by step 2.3 and $\Pi(V_\eta)\le1$.

On valid posterior fibres, split the likelihood numerator over the test and its complement. The posterior formula [F7] gives $\Pi_n(V_\eta\mid X_{1:n})\le\widetilde\phi_n+A_n/D_n$, where $A_n:=(1-\widetilde\phi_n)\int_{V_\eta}\prod_{i=1}^n[p(\theta,X_i)/p_0(X_i)]\,\Pi(d\theta)$. Step 3.1 ensures the denominator is finite and positive for all sufficiently large $n$ almost surely.

Choose $0<a<b<c$ and use step 3.1 with these radii. Since $c>0$ and $c-b>0$, [F27] gives $e^{-c},e^{-(c-b)}\in(0,1)$; [F28] makes the corresponding geometric series finite. For each $r>0$, Markov [F15] gives $\sum_{n\ge m}P_0^n(e^{nb}A_n>r)\le r^{-1}e^{1/8}\sum_{n\ge m}e^{-n(c-b)}<\infty$. Borel–Cantelli [F16], first for $r=1/k$ and then by countability, gives $e^{nb}A_n\to0$ almost surely. The type-I bound from step 2.3 is also summable, so [F16] gives $\widetilde\phi_n\to0$ almost surely. Combining these limits with $D_n\ge\Pi(B_a)e^{-nb}$ from step 3.1 and step 4.1 proves $\Pi_n(V_\eta\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ almost surely.
The consistency conclusion holds simultaneously for all $\eta>0$: intersect the probability-one events for positive rational $q$; for any $\eta>0$ choose rational $q<\eta$, so $V_\eta\subseteq V_q$.

For each $\theta$ with finite KL, Pinsker [F17] and the local comparison [F18] give $h(P_0,P_\theta)^2\le2\sqrt{D(P_0\|P_\theta)/2}$, hence $h(P_0,P_\theta)^4\le2D(P_0\|P_\theta)$. The parameter map $\theta\mapsto h(P_0,P_\theta)^2$ is measurable: [F25] makes both square-root sections measurable, [F23] makes their squared difference product-measurable, and Tonelli [F6] makes its $\mu$-integral measurable in $\theta$. Thus every Hellinger ball is measurable. Taking a positive-measure KL subset $B_{\eta^4/2}$ places it inside $\{\theta:h(P_0,P_\theta)<\eta\}$, proving positive prior mass.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in

maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$

$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).

measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$

parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,

$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$

subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\mathsf X=\{0,1\}$ with counting measure, let $\Theta=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, and put $\delta_k=(k+2)^{-2}$ for $k\ge1$. Define $P_0=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ and $P_k=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2+\delta_k)$. Every mass is strictly between zero and one, and the map $k\mapsto P_k$ is injective because the $\delta_k$ are distinct. Thus the model is identifiable by [F1]. The parameter and observation spaces are discrete, so every event-probability section is measurable by [F9] and every function on their countable product, including the pointwise Bernoulli density, is jointly measurable. The counting measure is sigma-finite and the displayed densities are normalized, so this is a dominated model by [F8].

Give the true parameter $0$ prior mass zero and set $\Pi(\{k\})=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$. By [F10] these masses sum to one, so [F12] makes $\Pi$ a probability. For $\delta=\delta_k$, the explicit densities and [F2] give $D(P_0\|P_k)=\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1/2+\delta}+\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1/2-\delta}=-\tfrac12\log(1-4\delta^2)$. For $0<x<1$, [F11] gives $0\le-\log(1-x)=\int_{1-x}^1dt/t\le x/(1-x)$; hence $0\le D(P_0\|P_k)\le2\delta_k^2/(1-4\delta_k^2)\to0$. Every KL neighborhood of $P_0$ therefore contains some $P_k$ with prior mass $2^{-k}>0$.

Put $d(P_j,P_k)=1$ for distinct model laws and $d(P_j,P_j)=0$. This is a metric: if the endpoints in a triangle inequality differ, at least one adjacent pair differs and the sum of its two distances is at least one; if they agree, the left side is zero. Thus the parameter complement is $V_{1/2}=\{k\ge1\}$. For every finite data vector, all $P_k^n(x_{1:n})>0$ and are at most one, so the evidence $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}P_k^n(x_{1:n})$ is finite and positive. By [F5], the posterior is supported on $\{k\ge1\}$; consequently $\Pi_n(V_{1/2}\mid x_{1:n})=1$ for every data vector and every $n$.

Let $\rho_k=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}}\sqrt{P_0(\{x\})P_k(\{x\})}$. Then $0\le\rho_k\le1$, since $h(P_0,P_k)^2=2-2\rho_k$ is an integral of a square. The IID product law [F6, F7] and distributivity give product affinity $\rho_k^n$, so $h(P_0^n,P_k^n)^2=2(1-\rho_k^n)\le n\,2(1-\rho_k)=n h(P_0,P_k)^2$, since $1-r^n=(1-r)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r^j\le n(1-r)$ for $0\le r\le1$. Also $\|P_0-P_k\|_{\rm TV}=\delta_k$: the four events in $\{0,1\}$ have probability differences $0,\delta_k,-\delta_k,0$. Thus [F3] gives $\|P_0^n-P_n^n\|_{\rm TV}\le h(P_0^n,P_n^n)\le\sqrt{2n\delta_n}\to0$.

Write $\Delta_n(x)=P_0^n(\{x\})-P_n^n(\{x\})$ on the finite sample space. Since $\sum_x\Delta_n(x)=0$, the positive and negative sums each have magnitude $\|P_0^n-P_n^n\|_{\rm TV}$: the event $\{x:\Delta_n(x)>0\}$ attains the positive sum, and every event sum lies between the negative and positive sums. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. For supplied finite-valued nonnegative measurable density representatives $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ in the convention of [[def-likelihood-density]], the **root-L2 Hellinger distance** is

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC for the imported density-representative convention. Let $P,Q$ be probability laws on a measurable space, both dominated by one specified common sigma-finite positive measure. Then the root-L2 Hellinger distance from [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]] is independent of the choice of common dominating measure. With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q),\qquad h(P,Q)^2\le 2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$

By [F1], $h(P,Q)^2=(\sqrt1-\sqrt0)^2+(\sqrt0-\sqrt1)^2=2$, so $h(P,Q)=\sqrt2$. Therefore $h(P,Q)^2=2\,\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)$, attaining equality in the upper comparison in [F3]; the lower comparison reads $1\le\sqrt2$.
